/SUNDAY NIGHT THROUGH FRIDAY/...
Issued at 145 PM CDT Fri Oct 30 2026

Gusty southerly winds on Monday, preceding the next system:

On Monday, a deep and energetic trough that had been progressing
through the west CONUS during the day Sunday will kick off deep
surface cyclogenesis across the north-central Plains. This
create a strong mass response, tightening the surface pressure 
gradient, and increasing southerly wind speeds across the area.
Forecasted sustained wind speeds are at 15-25 mph with the NBM
showing a >80% chance for frequent gusts above 30, and a 15-25%
chance for a few gusts up to 40 mph. While this will be quite
windier than what we've had throughout the summer, it is still
expected to be below Wind Advisory threshold, with only a less
than 10% chance for gusts to exceed the threshold.


Widespread band of rain expected Monday night through Tuesday:

The strong surface winds will finally pump in some appreciable
surface moisture to the area, with dewpoints reaching the middle
60s Monday, amid highs still in the middle 70s. The energetic
nature of the wave will bring strong and widespread synoptic
lift over the moisture, with a surface front clearing through
the warm sector. This will bring high certainty in seeing
widespread rain with the system Monday night through Tuesday
(90-95% chance).

Ensemble clusters are slowly coming into agreement on the nature
of the system, with only slight disagreements in timing and
exact location. Therefore, rain chances are near certain, with
each cluster having a mean precipitation amount of at least
0.75-1.00 inches across the area. The slight disagreements,
though, produce uncertainty in potential higher amounts. If
enough instability can reach into the area, thunderstorms within
the band of rain could lead to localized amounts up to 3-4
inches in some spots (90th percentile of NBM). The system is
expected to be very progressive, though, and with the D3-D4
Drought in place, the flooding threat will be minimal even with
the higher amounts in play. 


Monitoring low-end severe weather potential with the system:

With lots of jet stream energy attending the system, wind shear
will be bountiful (40-60 kts of deep-layer shear). Instability
is a big question, though, depending on the exact position and
timing of the trough. The most likely scenario currently depicts
the greatest severe risk Monday being across Kansas and Oklahoma
where the current SPC Day 4 15% Outlook is in place. The
boundary of this outlook is just west of our southeast Kansas
counties. Looking at LREF clusters, there's a decent chance
(40-50%) for MUCAPE to be above 250 J/kg as the front moves into
our area late Monday night. This could be enough for a high-
shear, low-CAPE severe setup. However, the threat would be
dwindling as it enters our area with instability decreasing
through the night.

With this most likely scenario, Tuesday's threat would also be
up in the air. The timing of the system would place any
appreciable rebound instability on our far eastern ends of the
area Tuesday afternoon. Which would keep the severe risk east
of the area. AI guidance does show this "hop" scenario. Of
course, there are clusters that depict a slower or faster wave
progression which would modify any risk. On that same line, a
further south or north position of the trough axis would present
more or less instability, also altering the threat. Therefore,
expect changes in the forecast as we get closer to the event.
Bottom line is at least Marginal threat for a line of low-topped
strong storms appears the most likely scenario given the current
model guidance.


Dry and slightly above normal temperatures to follow:

The cold front attending the strong wave is actually not
expected to be that cold. Temperatures are forecast to only
marginally drop into the 60s for Wednesday and Thursday, with
lows in the 40s.
